passage:
Dear Darshan,

You asked why I disappeared from the group call last night. Honestly, I was in the storeroom for ten minutes. Since the product launch began, I have noticed something odd: whenever a deadline closes in, my cheeks go hard, like I am holding water in my mouth, and then I let out a long puffed breath without meaning to. Yesterday I caught it in the dark screen of my laptop and thought, that is not a face that can review anyone's code. So I stood up, drank water by the window, and stretched my shoulders. I came back calmer, though still tired. Next time, if I look like that, please just ask if I need a minute. 🙂

Urmila

qa.q: Where did Urmila go during the group call?
qa.a: Urmila went to the storeroom for ten minutes.

qa.q: What did the hard cheeks and puffed breath most likely tell Urmila, and what else could they mean?
qa.a: Most likely they told Urmila that the launch deadlines had left tension and tiredness in the body, which is why a break was needed. They could also have been a simple habit or a reaction to the stuffy room, but Urmila read them as stress.

qa.q: What could Darshan do the next time Urmila's face looks like that?
qa.a: Darshan could quietly ask whether Urmila needs a minute, as requested, and not comment on the mood in front of others.

qa.q: How might Darshan have seen Urmila leaving the call?
qa.a: Darshan may have thought Urmila was avoiding work or was upset with the team, since the cheeks and breathing were out of sight and only the absence was noticed.

grounding: Illustrates an adult noticing clenched cheeks and a puffed breath under stress and taking a short break, with a request for gentle support from others.

subtype: Cheek movement in fatigue and stress [Regulating]
passage: So Maria, you asked how I knew I was cracking. It was my cheeks, honestly. I run the pharmacy's billing desk, and in month-end week my face goes tight, cheeks clenched, then this big puff of air like a small balloon leaking. I am Dilnaz, by the way. My cousin Zoya pointed it out once. She said, you look like you are about to fight the printer. Now when I feel my jaw and cheeks lock, I step outside for five slow breaths and drink some water. Does it fix the workload? No. But I return less snappy, and the queue is still there, still manageable. 😅

qa.q: Which job does Dilnaz do?
qa.a: She runs the billing desk at a pharmacy.

qa.a: It suggests she treats the tight cheeks and puffed breath as a warning that she is strained, and she chooses a short pause to ease it. The alternative is that she is simply hot or short of air, but her own explanation points to month-end stress.

qa.q: What does Dilnaz's routine show about handling stress, and where does it fall short?
qa.a: It gives her a small reset so she returns less snappy, but she says herself it does not reduce the workload, so she might also ask for help or share the month-end tasks.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's cousin Zoya have felt pointing this out?
qa.a: Zoya probably meant it lightly and with care, since she used a joke about the printer, though Dilnaz could have felt embarrassed at first.

grounding: Illustrates an adult who notices tense cheeks and a puffed breath in herself and uses a short break to settle.

subtype: Cheek movement in fatigue and stress [Regulating]
passage: Yusuf here, at the desk across from Kalyani in the logistics office. Thursday was the day forty trucks got rerouted because of the flooded highway. By noon I noticed her cheeks drawn in tight, like she was biting the insides of them, and every few minutes she blew out a long breath that puffed her whole face out. I couldn't tell if she was angry at the drivers, at our manager, or just worn out. Then she pushed back her chair, said "Five minutes," and walked to the window by the water cooler. She stood there rolling her shoulders and looking at the rain. When she came back, her jaw looked looser. I slid a printout of the pending routes onto her desk and asked, "Want me to take the southern ones?" She nodded. "Yes. Thank you."

qa.a: Forty trucks got rerouted because of the flooded highway.

qa.q: What might Kalyani's drawn-in cheeks and puffed breaths suggest about how she was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely she was tense and stressed by the rerouting rush; it could also have been anger at someone or plain tiredness, which Yusuf could not tell apart.

qa.q: Which choice helped Kalyani, and why?
qa.a: Taking five minutes at the window and rolling her shoulders let the tension ease, so she came back looser and could accept help.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see Kalyani's stress, and how does Yusuf respond?
qa.a: Yusuf notices the cues but isn't sure what they mean, so instead of guessing, Yusuf offers practical help by taking the southern routes.

passage:
Monday: In the lift mirror, Lalremsiami caught her own face: cheeks sucked in hard, then a big puff of air out. Three site drawings were due Friday. She looked away, went back to her desk and ate lunch over the keyboard.
Wednesday: The same puff escaped her during a client call, and this time she noticed it. She finished the call, set a five-minute timer and walked the stairwell up and down, loosening her face with a few slow breaths. The drawings still waited, but her hand on the mouse felt steadier.
The next Tuesday: Across the table, Jaya kept blowing out her cheeks at a spreadsheet. Lalremsiami didn't comment on her face. She just put a cup of lemon tea by Jaya's elbow and said, "Stairwell walk in ten? I'll come." Jaya laughed, a little surprised, and said yes.

qa.q: How many site drawings were due on Friday?
qa.a: Three site drawings were due Friday.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling on Monday when she saw her face in the lift mirror?
qa.a: She was most likely stressed and tense about the drawings; the clenched cheeks might also have been simple tiredness, but she brushed it aside either way.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: On Wednesday she noticed the puff and took a five-minute stairwell walk with slow breaths, which left her steadier instead of pushing on while tense.

qa.q: What might it be like for Jaya when Lalremsiami offers tea and a walk?
qa.a: Jaya may feel surprised and cared for, because the support comes without anyone pointing out her face or making her feel watched.

grounding: Illustrates noticing stress-driven cheek clenching in oneself, taking a short break, and later offering gentle support to a colleague.

subtype: Cheek movement in fatigue and stress [Regulating]
passage: You keep puffing your cheeks at that screen, Parveen. Let me, Thomas, tell you about when I was twenty-five and new at the railway booking counter in Kochi. Festival rush, queues out to the road. By evening I'd clenched my cheeks so hard my teeth ached, and I blew out air between every passenger. One evening Mrs. D'Souza from the next window propped a card on my glass: "Counter closed, ten minutes." I was annoyed. I thought she was saying I was slow. She only said, "Your face has been fighting all day. Go and drink some water." I went. Standing outside, I felt my whole jaw unclench. After that I took those ten minutes myself, before anyone had to prop a card. Years later, when a young clerk under me started puffing like that, I put the same card on his glass.

qa.q: Where did Thomas work at twenty-five?
qa.a: At the railway booking counter in Kochi.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when Mrs. D'Souza put the card on the glass?
qa.a: Thomas felt annoyed and a little judged, reading it as a comment on being slow; it was really meant as care, which Thomas understood only after the break.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Thomas handled stress?
qa.a: Going outside for the ten minutes and feeling the jaw unclench; after that Thomas took the break without waiting for anyone to step in.

qa.q: How might Mrs. D'Souza have seen Thomas during the festival rush?
qa.a: She probably saw a young colleague worn down by the queues, a face 'fighting all day', and chose a quiet, practical way to give a break instead of a lecture.

grounding: An elder recalls clenched cheeks and puffed breaths under festival-rush stress, a colleague's gentle support, and learning to take a short break.

subtype: Cheek movement in fatigue and stress [Regulating]
passage:
The generator at the printing press had failed at four, and Rafiq had until nine to get two thousand exam booklets bound for the district office. Under the one working tube light, he puffed out a long breath, cheeks ballooning, then clenched his jaw so hard the muscles in his cheeks jumped.
Sabina, feeding covers into the stapler, glanced up. "That's the third time you've done the balloon face."
"What face?"
She puffed her own cheeks to show him. He laughed despite himself, then noticed how tight his face felt, like a fist.
"Five minutes," Sabina said. "Go stand outside. I'll keep stapling."
He stood by the gate in the drizzle, let his jaw hang loose and breathed slowly. When he came back, he spotted the missing box of covers he had walked past twice.

qa.q: How many exam booklets did Rafiq need to get bound?
qa.a: Rafiq had to get two thousand exam booklets bound for the district office.

qa.q: What did Rafiq's puffed cheeks and clenched jaw suggest?
qa.a: They suggested Rafiq was tense and stressed about the nine o'clock deadline; they might also have shown plain tiredness after the power failed.

qa.q: What small step helped Rafiq get back on track?
qa.a: A five-minute break outside, letting his jaw loosen and breathing slowly, cleared his head enough to spot the missing box of covers.

qa.q: How did Sabina see the balloon face?
qa.a: Sabina read it as a sign he was strained, so she mirrored it back lightly and kept stapling so he could step out.

grounding: Puffed cheeks and a clenched jaw signal stress; noticing them leads to a short break, and a colleague offers gentle support.
